headline: Apollo's chief economist, Torsten Slok, warned that the AI boom is drawing capital, power and workers away from the rest of the US economy.
score_reason: Pool 5 kept: a clear argument from a named economist, reported by one outlet from his note rather than from new data.
importance_line: Households and firms tied to housing and cars face interest rates that may stay high because AI spending is not slowing, which also complicates the Federal Reserve's task; it is one economist's analysis, and an earlier note of his cautions that the build-out could unwind just as fast if demand disappoints.
summary: Stocktwits reports, in an article carried by Yahoo Finance, that Torsten Slok, chief economist at the investment firm Apollo Global Management, wrote in a note on Friday 9 Oct that AI spending is absorbing capital, electricity and workers at a pace that could leave other sectors struggling to compete, a pattern he calls 'Dutch disease' (a boom in one sector that pulls resources from others), while housing and autos are squeezed by high interest rates that have not slowed the AI build-out. He argues this makes it harder for the Federal Reserve to cool the economy and could keep rates higher for longer, and that 'the only durable fix is expanding the supply of power, chips and infrastructure'.
notes: Read on the Yahoo Finance copy of the Stocktwits article; url is Stocktwits' own link. The note is dated Friday 9 Oct and was first reported on 10 Oct; no earlier edition carried it.
